meta.title: Swahili B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Swahili → English (see the Swahili, recall the meaning) and English → Swahili (see an English meaning, recall the Swahili). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise whilst travelling, to produce simple connected text on topics which are familiar or of personal interest, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Swahili that could be used here, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 225 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and the office, study and learning, news and the media, travel and accommodation, nature and the environment, society and the state, relationships and life events, feelings and opinions, talking and arguing, the everyday verbs of these, the abstract nouns opinions are built from, health and emergencies, sport and the arts, crime and the law, housing and money, character and values, size and measure, describing, time and sequence, and the words that join an argument together — and the other 775 are the commonest remaining words, counted by the WHOLE word (every form of a noun, every conjugated form of a verb added together) in two collections of real Swahili, film and television subtitles and the Global Voices news site, a word having to be common in both. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Verbs are shown as their infinitive (kusoma, to read) with their stem (-soma), which every tense is built on, and their negative infinitive; adjectives and possessives as their stem (-zuri, -angu) with the forms they take after three of the noun classes. The 611 nouns show their class, which every adjective, verb and possessive agrees with, and their plural; there are 308 verbs. Real example sentences come with 641 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 248 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted from OpenSubtitles 2024 and Global Voices (CC BY 3.0), both as distributed by OPUS. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
